Overview When recent unauthenticated PHP RCE advisories dropped (targeting PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and oversized request bodies), I was in the middle of auditing several inherited Linux web servers I took over following a team retirement.
While we work through a broader migration to move legacy workloads onto fresh, Terraform-managed infrastructure, I wanted to immediately reduce our PHP attack surface and add defense-in-depth controls across the existing hosts—without causing production downtime.
Because I was working across live systems that lacked a 1:1 staging twin, I leaned heavily on Claude Code and AWS Systems Manager (SSM) to orchestrate the discovery, build hash-checked apply/rollback scripts, and run an automated curl verification suite after every change. Here is how we locked the environment down.
1. Turning Off PHP Where It Isn’t Needed The best way to reduce PHP risk on an inherited server is to verify whether the host actually needs PHP running at all:
Reverse Proxy Nodes: During read-only discovery, I found Nginx configurations still wired to pass *.php requests to an active php-fpm pool for a legacy management tool that was no longer used. We backed up and removed the PHP location blocks, reloaded Nginx gracefully, and masked the service (systemctl mask php-fpm) so it can’t be started accidentally. Non-PHP Application Servers: Even when a core web application doesn’t use PHP, default Apache php.conf packages often globally route any *.php request (including nonexistent URLs) to php-fpm. We disabled the global handler, denied .php execution across public document roots, and restricted internal database utilities strictly to VPN subnets. 2. Hardening Public PHP Workloads Where PHP was legitimately required for public-facing web properties, we layered multiple controls at both the web server and the PHP-FPM pool:
Removed legacy surface area: Used <LocationMatch> at the server config level (which cannot be overridden by .htaccess files in the web root) to block legacy diagnostic scripts and restrict non-production vhosts strictly to internal VPN traffic. Enforced strict request body limits: Configured LimitRequestBody in Apache alongside matching SecRequestBodyLimit caps in ModSecurity so oversized POST payloads are dropped at the edge before reaching PHP. Locked down the PHP-FPM pool: Set expose_php = Off to stop broadcasting version headers and enforced php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off in the pool config. Using php_admin_flag ensures that neither .htaccess nor runtime ini_set() calls can re-enable session upload progress. 3. Catching the 1,001-Argument ModSecurity Bypass To block exploit attempts before they reached PHP-FPM, we added a ModSecurity virtual patch to deny any request containing the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS parameter.
Standard exploit tests immediately returned 403 Forbidden. Then we tested an edge case: what happens if an attacker stuffs a POST request with 1,000 junk parameters and puts the malicious trigger as the 1,001st parameter?
In our initial test, it bypassed the WAF rule and returned 200 OK.
Digging into the legacy ModSecurity configuration revealed why:
SecArgumentsLimit was set to 1000. Years earlier, a previous admin had added SecRuleRemoveById 200001—disabling the stock ModSecurity rule that rejects requests when the body parser hits a limit (REQBODY_ERROR), likely to work around false positives on complex content uploads. Because rule 200001 was disabled, ModSecurity simply stopped inspecting parameters after argument 1,000 and passed the rest of the request through to Apache.
The Fix: After running a log-only rule to verify normal traffic patterns, we deployed a strict enforcement rule returning 400 Bad Request on any REQBODY_ERROR (any unparseable body or >1,000 arguments). Re-running the 1,001-argument test immediately flipped the response from 200 OK to 400 Bad Request.
4. Hardening systemd Against Scanner OOM Spikes Vulnerability disclosures always bring waves of aggressive internet scanning, which can easily trigger Out-Of-Memory (OOM) events on smaller instances. During our audit, we noticed two dangerous default settings:
Several services were running with the default Restart=no policy—meaning if systemd-oomd killed the web server during a traffic spike, it would stay down until manually restarted. php-fpm defaulted to OOMPolicy=stop, meaning a single OOM-killed worker process could take down the entire PHP pool. We deployed systemd drop-in overrides (10-restart.conf) across the fleet setting Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=5s, and OOMPolicy=continue, and removed an unused legacy background agent to free up system memory. Testing with kill -9 confirmed the web daemon recovered automatically in under 6 seconds.
Orchestrating Changes Safely with Claude Code Making dozens of web server, WAF, and systemd changes across live production servers requires tight guardrails. Rather than hand-editing config files over SSH, I used Claude Code to help build a structured deployment workflow over AWS SSM:
Read-Only Discovery First: Every step started with non-destructive SSM scripts checking active listeners, file checksums, and weeks of access logs to confirm nothing legitimate would break. Hash-Guarded Apply & Rollback Scripts: Every change was packaged as a paired apply.sh and rollback.sh. Scripts verified the SHA-256 hash of existing config files before making changes, used drop-in files (zz-*.conf) instead of editing base configs wherever possible, and verified apachectl configtest / nginx -t before reloading. Automated Regression Suite: We built a 50+ check bash test harness that verified public pages, authentication flows, request size caps, and our ModSecurity bypass tests before and after every single step. Forty-eight hours after wrapping up the deployment, automated scanners swept across our public IPs firing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS payloads. Every probe was dropped at the edge with a 403, with zero worker crashes or false positives.

Here is how we locked the environment down.

Overview Offboarding is one of those tasks that’s simple on paper and easy to get subtly wrong in practice. Miss a step and you end up with a departed user who still has an active session token, a mailbox nobody can read, or a license you’re paying for months later.
Between employees and a steady rotation of contractors, I was offboarding people often enough that a checklist in my head wasn’t good enough. This post walks through the script I use now. It takes a UPN and runs the whole sequence the same way every time.
The Checklist Here’s the sequence the script automates, in this order:
Disable sign-in. Revoke all refresh tokens and sessions. Convert the mailbox to a shared mailbox and hide it from the address list. Give the user’s manager Full Access to the mailbox. Remove the user from cloud groups. Remove directly assigned licenses. Email an “offboarding complete” summary to HR and the manager. The order matters. If you remove the Exchange license before converting the mailbox to shared, the mailbox starts down the path to being disabled. Convert first, then pull licenses.
Prerequisites Install-Module Microsoft.Graph -Scope CurrentUser Install-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement -Scope CurrentUser If you use Privileged Identity Management (PIM), activate these roles before running the script:
Role Why the script needs it User Administrator Disable the account, remove licenses, and manage group membership Authentication Administrator Revoke sign-in sessions and refresh tokens Exchange Administrator Convert the mailbox, set permissions, and manage distribution lists The Graph connection also requests Mail.Send so the script can send the confirmation email from your account. The first run will prompt you to consent to that scope.
The Script <# .SYNOPSIS Offboards a Microsoft 365 user: disable, revoke, convert mailbox, delegate to manager, remove groups and licenses, then email HR and the manager a confirmation. .EXAMPLE .\Invoke-M365Offboarding.ps1 -UserPrincipalName jdoe@example.com -WhatIf .EXAMPLE .\Invoke-M365Offboarding.ps1 -UserPrincipalName jdoe@example.com -HrAddress hr@example.com #> [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)] param( [Parameter(Mandatory)] [string]$UserPrincipalName, # Optional override if the manager isn't set in Entra ID [string]$DelegateTo, # Where the confirmation email goes (in addition to the manager) [string]$HrAddress = 'hr@example.com' ) $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' $log = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new() Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'User.ReadWrite.All','Group.ReadWrite.All','Directory.ReadWrite.All','Mail.Send' -NoWelcome Connect-ExchangeOnline -ShowBanner:$false $user = Get-MgUser -UserId $UserPrincipalName -Property Id,DisplayName,UserPrincipalName,AssignedLicenses # Resolve the manager (used for mailbox delegation and the confirmation email) $managerUpn = $null try { $mgr = Get-MgUserManager -UserId $user.Id $managerUpn = $mgr.AdditionalProperties['userPrincipalName'] } catch { Write-Warning 'No manager set in Entra ID.' } if (-not $DelegateTo) { $DelegateTo = $managerUpn } if (-not $DelegateTo) { Write-Warning 'No delegate found; mailbox will not be delegated.' } # 1-2. Disable sign-in and revoke sessions if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($UserPrincipalName, 'Disable account and revoke sessions')) { Update-MgUser -UserId $user.Id -AccountEnabled:$false Revoke-MgUserSignInSession -UserId $user.Id | Out-Null $log.Add('The account has been disabled and all sign-in sessions have been revoked.') } # 3. Convert the mailbox to shared and hide it from the GAL if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($UserPrincipalName, 'Convert mailbox to shared')) { Set-Mailbox -Identity $UserPrincipalName -Type Shared Set-Mailbox -Identity $UserPrincipalName -HiddenFromAddressListsEnabled $true $log.Add('The mailbox has been converted to a shared mailbox and hidden from the address list.') } # 4. Delegate mailbox access if ($DelegateTo -and $PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($UserPrincipalName, "Grant Full Access to $DelegateTo")) { Add-MailboxPermission -Identity $UserPrincipalName -User $DelegateTo ` -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All -AutoMapping $true | Out-Null $log.Add("$DelegateTo has been granted access to the mailbox.") } # 5. Remove cloud group memberships (skip dynamic and mail-enabled groups) $groups = Get-MgUserMemberOf -UserId $user.Id -All | Where-Object { $_.AdditionalProperties['@odata.type'] -eq '#microsoft.graph.group' } foreach ($g in $groups) { $types = $g.AdditionalProperties['groupTypes'] $mail = $g.AdditionalProperties['mailEnabled'] $isUnified = $types -contains 'Unified' $isDynamic = $types -contains 'DynamicMembership' $name = $g.AdditionalProperties['displayName'] if ($isDynamic) { continue } # membership is rule-based if ($mail -and -not $isUnified) { # Distribution lists / mail-enabled security groups are managed in Exchange if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($name, 'Remove from distribution group')) { Remove-DistributionGroupMember -Identity $g.AdditionalProperties['mail'] -Member $UserPrincipalName ` -BypassSecurityGroupManagerCheck -Confirm:$false } } elseif ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($name, 'Remove from group')) { Remove-MgGroupMemberByRef -GroupId $g.Id -DirectoryObjectId $user.Id } } # 6. Remove directly assigned licenses (after mailbox conversion) $skuIds = @($user.AssignedLicenses.SkuId) if ($skuIds.Count -and $PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($UserPrincipalName, 'Remove licenses')) { try { Set-MgUserLicense -UserId $user.Id -AddLicenses @() -RemoveLicenses $skuIds | Out-Null } catch { Write-Warning "Some licenses may be group-assigned and were removed with group membership: $_" } } if (-not $WhatIfPreference) { $log.Add('Group memberships and licenses have been removed.') } # 7. Build the summary and email HR and the manager $summary = @" This is to confirm that $($user.DisplayName) ($UserPrincipalName) has been offboarded as of $(Get-Date -Format 'MM-dd-yyyy'). $(($log | ForEach-Object { " * $_" }) -join "`n") "@ $recipients = @($HrAddress, $managerUpn) | Where-Object { $_ } | Select-Object -Unique if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess(($recipients -join ', '), 'Send offboarding confirmation')) { $mail = @{ Message = @{ Subject = "Offboarding complete: $($user.DisplayName)" Body = @{ ContentType = 'Text'; Content = $summary } ToRecipients = @($recipients | ForEach-Object { @{ EmailAddress = @{ Address = $_ } } }) } SaveToSentItems = $true } $sender = (Get-MgContext).Account Send-MgUserMail -UserId $sender -BodyParameter $mail Write-Host "Confirmation sent to: $($recipients -join ', ')" } $summary Things the Script Handles (and Why) Revoking sessions, not just disabling. Disabling an account stops new sign-ins, but an existing refresh token can keep an app session alive for a while. Revoke-MgUserSignInSession invalidates those tokens so access ends now, not eventually.
Distribution lists vs. Microsoft 365 groups. Microsoft Graph can’t change membership of distribution lists or mail-enabled security groups. Those still live in Exchange. The script checks mailEnabled and groupTypes and sends each group to the right cmdlet.
Dynamic groups are skipped. Their membership is rule-based, and disabling the account (or changing attributes) takes care of them.
Group-based licensing. If licenses are assigned through a group, Set-MgUserLicense can’t remove them directly. They drop off when the user leaves the group. The try/catch keeps the script from stopping on that case.
Emailing HR and the manager. The script sends the summary from the signed-in admin’s mailbox with Send-MgUserMail, to the HR address and the manager from Entra ID, and keeps a copy in Sent Items as a record. If no manager is set, HR still gets the email. With -WhatIf, it shows who would be emailed without sending anything.
-WhatIf support. SupportsShouldProcess means I can dry-run against a real user and see exactly what would happen before committing. I always run it with -WhatIf first.
What’s Still Manual (For Now) A script shouldn’t pretend it handles everything. These are still on my checklist outside the script:
Devices: retire or wipe the user’s laptop in Intune and arrange its return. OneDrive: confirm the manager has access before the retention window closes. Microsoft 365 can grant this automatically if OneDrive retention and manager access is configured in the SharePoint admin center. Third-party apps that don’t use SSO, plus any shared credentials the user knew. Timing: for contractors, I schedule the run for the end of their final day rather than the morning of. Lessons Learned Order of operations matters. Converting the mailbox before removing licenses is the step people most often get backwards. Make it boring. The value of the script isn’t speed. It’s that the hundredth offboarding happens exactly like the first. Close the loop automatically. Sending the confirmation straight to HR and the manager means nobody has to ask whether it’s done, and the Sent Items copy doubles as an audit trail. Least privilege, just in time. Running under PIM-activated roles means the script only has admin rights for the window you actually need them.
summary:
Overview Offboarding is one of those tasks that’s simple on paper and easy to get subtly wrong in practice. Miss a step and you end up with a departed user who still has an active session token, a mailbox nobody can read, or a license you’re paying for months later.
Between employees and a steady rotation of contractors, I was offboarding people often enough that a checklist in my head wasn’t good enough. This post walks through the script I use now. It takes a UPN and runs the whole sequence the same way every time.
title: A Repeatable Microsoft 365 Offboarding Script with Graph PowerShell

Overview In an earlier post I set up SAML and MFA for VPN on a Cisco Firepower 1120 running ASA. Once that was in place, the next question was obvious: how do I know when something is wrong with the firewall without logging into ASDM every morning?
We already ran most of our infrastructure in AWS, so Amazon CloudWatch was the natural place to land firewall logs. The first attempt worked, and it also sent everything. The log volume was noisy, expensive to keep, and useless for alerting. This post covers the version I ended up with: a small Linux syslog relay, a trimmed log stream, and a handful of metric filters that drive alarms and a dashboard.
Architecture Cisco ASA (Firepower 1120) │ syslog (UDP 514) ▼ Linux relay (rsyslog) ──► /var/log/cisco/asa.log │ amazon-cloudwatch-agent ▼ CloudWatch Logs ──► Metric filters ──► Alarms (SNS) + Dashboard The relay can be any small Linux host the firewall can reach. I reused an existing utility server that already had the CloudWatch agent installed.
Step 1: Point the ASA at the Relay From the ASA CLI (or the equivalent in ASDM under Device Management → Logging):
logging enable logging timestamp logging device-id hostname logging host inside 10.0.0.25 logging trap warnings A few notes:
logging trap sets the severity sent to the syslog server. My first pass used informational, which includes every connection build and teardown. That was the main source of noise. Moving to warnings cut volume dramatically while keeping denies, threat detection, and failures. If you need a specific informational message (for example, AAA rejects for VPN logins, which are severity 6), you can raise just that message instead of lowering the whole trap level: logging message 113005 level warnings Step 2: Receive and Separate the Logs with rsyslog On the relay, enable UDP input and write ASA traffic to its own file so it doesn’t mix with system logs. ASA sends on facility local4 by default.
/etc/rsyslog.d/30-cisco-asa.conf:
module(load="imudp") input(type="imudp" port="514") if $syslogfacility-text == 'local4' then { action(type="omfile" file="/var/log/cisco/asa.log") stop } sudo mkdir -p /var/log/cisco sudo systemctl restart rsyslog Make sure the relay’s host firewall and any AWS security group only allow UDP 514 from the firewall’s address. You don’t want an open syslog listener.
Add a logrotate entry for /var/log/cisco/asa.log too. The CloudWatch agent handles rotation fine, but your disk won’t appreciate an unrotated firewall log.
Step 3: Ship the File with the CloudWatch Agent Add the log file to the agent’s collect_list in /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json:
{ "logs": { "logs_collected": { "files": { "collect_list": [ { "file_path": "/var/log/cisco/asa.log", "log_group_name": "/network/cisco-asa", "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}", "retention_in_days": 90 } ] } } } } Reload the agent:
sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \ -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s \ -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json Setting retention_in_days matters. CloudWatch Logs defaults to never expiring, and that’s where a noisy log group quietly becomes a line item.
Step 4: Turn Important Events into Metrics Logs are for investigating. Metrics are for alerting. I created a metric filter for each type of event I actually wanted to be woken up for. For example, VPN authentication rejects:
aws logs put-metric-filter \ --log-group-name /network/cisco-asa \ --filter-name asa-aaa-reject \ --filter-pattern '"%ASA-4-113005"' \ --metric-transformations \ metricName=AaaAuthReject,metricNamespace=Network/ASA,metricValue=1,defaultValue=0 Because I raised message 113005 to warnings in Step 1, it arrives as %ASA-4-113005 rather than the default %ASA-6-113005. Match the pattern to the level you configured.
Other filters worth considering (verify the message IDs against your ASA version’s syslog reference):
What Pattern idea Threat detection rate exceeded "%ASA-4-733100" Denied inbound traffic "%ASA-2-106001" or "%ASA-4-106023" Any critical/alert/emergency "%ASA-1-", "%ASA-2-" Step 5: Alarms and a Dashboard An alarm on the auth-reject metric, sending to an SNS topic that emails the IT mailbox:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ --alarm-name asa-vpn-auth-rejects-high \ --namespace Network/ASA \ --metric-name AaaAuthReject \ --statistic Sum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 \ --threshold 10 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \ --treat-missing-data notBreaching \ --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-west-2:111122223333:it-alerts The thresholds are a judgment call. Start loose, watch a couple of weeks of data, then tighten. An alarm that fires every day gets ignored, which is worse than no alarm.
For the dashboard, I put the metric-filter graphs next to a Logs Insights widget that shows the most recent high-severity lines:
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /%ASA-[1-3]-/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20 Now the firewall’s morning check is a single CloudWatch dashboard tab.
A Side Fix: SIP Inspection While reviewing the running config, I also removed SIP inspection from the default policy. ASA’s SIP inspection is a well-known cause of odd VoIP and Wi-Fi calling behavior when you aren’t running an on-prem phone system through the firewall:
policy-map global_policy class inspection_default no inspect sip Test this in your environment first. If you do rely on the ASA to handle SIP, leave it on.
Lessons Learned Trim at the source. Lowering logging trap on the ASA did more for cost and clarity than any filtering downstream. Separate logs early. A dedicated file and log group per device type keeps metric filters simple. Set retention on day one. Never-expiring log groups are a slow-moving bill. Alert on metrics, investigate in logs. Metric filters turn a wall of text into a few numbers you can actually watch.

Overview Email is the one system nobody notices until it stops working. When we moved a 70-person company from Google Workspace to Exchange Online, the goal wasn’t just “move the mail.” It was to move the mail without anyone missing a message, a calendar invite, or an automated workflow that quietly depended on a Gmail inbox.
This post is the checklist I wish I’d had at the start. It’s written for small IT teams (often a team of one) doing a cutover without a migration partner.
1. Inventory Before You Touch DNS The mailboxes are the easy part. The things that break are everything around the mailboxes:
Shared inboxes and groups. Google Groups used as shared inboxes (support@, hr@, billing@) need a deliberate destination: an Exchange shared mailbox, a distribution list, or a Microsoft 365 group. Things that send mail. Copiers with scan-to-email, monitoring tools, line-of-business apps, and scripts that relay through Gmail SMTP. Automations that read mail. Any Power Automate flow, Zap, or script that triggers off a Gmail inbox. Block lists and filters. Senders you’ve blocked over the years live in Google’s admin console, not in your head. Who actually uses what. Some “users” are former employees, service accounts, or aliases that should become shared mailboxes or simply be archived. I put all of this in a SharePoint list with a column for “destination in M365” and “verified after cutover.” That list became the cutover runbook.
2. Build the Destination First Before migrating any data, I stood up the Exchange Online side completely:
Licensed user mailboxes for real people. Shared mailboxes for team inboxes. They don’t need a license under 50 GB, and access is managed by permission rather than password sharing. Distribution lists for simple fan-out addresses. Mail-enabled security groups only where something also needed SharePoint or app permissions. Getting the destination right first means users land in a finished environment instead of one that’s still being assembled around them.
3. Migrate in Batches I ran the mailbox data migration in batches from the Exchange admin center. The pattern that worked:
Pilot batch. IT plus one or two friendly power users. Validate mail, calendar, contacts, and labels-to-folders mapping. Bulk batches. Grouped by department so each team cut over together. Incremental syncs right up to the MX change, so the final delta was small. Expect at least one mailbox to get stuck. Mine was a sync issue on a large mailbox that needed a couple of re-runs. Leave yourself slack in the schedule for it.
4. Authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC This is where a lot of small migrations leave risk on the table. During coexistence, both Google and Microsoft may send as your domain, so your records need to reflect that, and then get tightened once Google is out of the path.
SPF, during coexistence:
example.com. TXT "v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com include:_spf.google.com -all" SPF, after cutover:
example.com. TXT "v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all" Don’t forget anything else that sends as your domain (a marketing platform, a ticketing system). Every one of those needs to be in SPF or sending through an authenticated path.
DKIM: In the Microsoft Defender portal, go to Email & collaboration → Policies & rules → Threat policies → Email authentication settings → DKIM. Microsoft gives you two CNAME records (selector1._domainkey and selector2._domainkey). Publish both exactly as shown, wait for DNS to propagate, then enable signing.
DMARC: Start in monitor mode so you can see who is sending as you before you start enforcing:
_dmarc.example.com. TXT "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com; fo=1" Once the aggregate reports show only legitimate senders passing, step up to p=quarantine, and eventually p=reject.
5. Don’t Forget the Block List Years of “please block this sender” requests lived in Google’s admin console. I exported them and re-created them in the Tenant Allow/Block List in Microsoft Defender. In Exchange Online PowerShell:
Connect-ExchangeOnline $blocked = Import-Csv .\google-blocked-senders.csv # column: Sender New-TenantAllowBlockListItems -ListType Sender -Block ` -Entries $blocked.Sender -NoExpiration This is a small step, but users notice immediately when spam they’d “already blocked” comes back.
6. Fix the Automations Several Power Automate flows triggered off a Google shared inbox. After cutover, each one had to be repointed to the new Exchange shared mailbox using the Office 365 Outlook trigger “When a new email arrives in a shared mailbox (V2).” Test every flow end to end with a real message, not just a “Save.”
The same goes for devices and apps that sent mail. I verified each relay path (scan-to-email, application notifications) by sending a real message and confirming delivery with message trace in the Exchange admin center.
7. Cutover Day Lower the MX record TTL a day or two ahead. Run the final incremental sync. Flip MX to Exchange Online Protection. Watch message trace and the quarantine for the first 24–48 hours. Legitimate mail caught by new filtering is the most common day-one complaint. Send users a short Outlook setup guide (desktop, mobile, and “where did my labels go?”). 8. Clean Up Google Afterward Once mail was flowing and users had settled in, I exported what needed to be retained and archived the majority of the Google accounts. That alone cut the next Google billing cycle by roughly $400, a nice way to close out the project with a visible win.
Lessons Learned The inventory is the project. The mailbox move is mostly mechanical. The surprises come from shared inboxes, relays, and automations. Treat DMARC as part of the migration, not a follow-up ticket. You’ll never have a better moment to get it right. Verify with message trace, not assumptions. “It should work” isn’t the same as a delivered message. Close the loop on cost. Archiving the old platform promptly turns a migration into a savings story.

Overview Setting up SAML authentication with MFA on a Cisco Firepower 1120 for VPN access is essential for modern security requirements. Microsoft’s documentation provides a good starting point, but it’s missing critical CLI configuration commands for the Firepower side.
This guide fills in those gaps and documents the lessons learned during implementation.
Prerequisites Cisco Firepower 1120 with appropriate licensing and AnyConnect Microsoft Entra ID tenant with administrative access Access to Firepower via ASDM or CLI Your Firepower VPN’s public FQDN and SSL certificate configured Configuration Steps Step 1: Create the Enterprise Application in Azure Follow Microsoft’s guide to create the Cisco Secure Firewall app in Microsoft Entra ID:
Sign in to the Azure portal Navigate to Microsoft Entra ID > Enterprise Applications Click New application > Create your own application Search for “Cisco Secure Firewall - Secure Client (Clientless VPN)” and add it Navigate to Single sign-on and select SAML Step 2: Configure SAML Settings in Azure Configure the basic SAML settings:
Identifier (Entity ID): https://[your-vpn-fqdn.domain.com] Reply URL (ACS): https://[your-vpn-fqdn.domain.com]/saml/acs Sign on URL: https://[your-vpn-fqdn.domain.com] Important: These URLs must exactly match your Firepower’s base URL configuration.
Step 3: Download the SAML Certificate In the Azure SAML configuration, scroll to SAML Signing Certificate Download the Certificate (Base64) Open the certificate file in a text editor - you’ll need this content for the CLI configuration Step 4: Note Your Azure Tenant ID You’ll need your Azure Tenant ID for the Firepower configuration:
Navigate to Microsoft Entra ID > Overview Copy your Tenant ID (it looks like: 12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789abc) Step 5: Configure Firepower SAML (The Missing Piece) Here’s the commands in one place with tabs and formatting for easy copy-paste. Edit the placeholders as needed.
config t crypto ca trustpoint [YourTrustpointName] revocation-check none no id-usage enrollment terminal no ca-check crypto ca authenticate [YourTrustpointName] -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- [Paste Base64 certificate from Azure here] -----END CERTIFICATE----- quit webvpn saml idp https://sts.windows.net/[AZURE-TENANT-ID]/ url sign-in https://login.microsoftonline.com/[AZURE-TENANT-ID]/saml2 url sign-out https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/wsfederation?wa=wsignout1.0 trustpoint idp [YourTrustpointName] trustpoint sp [YourFirewallSSLCertName] no force re-authentication no signature base-url https://[your-vpn-fqdn.domain.com] end write mem Configuration parameters:
[YourTrustpointName] - A descriptive name for the Microsoft Entra ID certificate (e.g., “EntraID-SAML”) [AZURE-TENANT-ID] - Your Azure tenant ID from Step 4 [YourFirewallSSLCertName] - The existing SSL certificate trustpoint name on your Firepower [your-vpn-fqdn.domain.com] - Your VPN’s public FQDN (must match Azure configuration) Step 6: Configure the Connection Profile in ASDM Open ASDM and navigate to Remote Access VPN > Network (Client) Access > AnyConnect Connection Profiles Create the connection profile using the endpoints from Azure. Assign a group policy. Click OK and Apply Lessons Learned 1. Redirect URL changes mean a new certificate I initially downloaded the SAML certificate when setting up the configuration. Later, I found a typo in my redirect URL and corrected it in Azure.
Critical lesson: Changing the redirect URL in Azure requires downloading a new SAML certificate and re-importing it into the Firepower. The certificate is tied to the specific URLs configured in Azure. Without the updated cert, the SAML handshake will fail with cryptic errors.
2. Applying SAML profile changes in ASDM The official guides don’t emphasize this, but if you update the SAML profile, you should disable and re-enable it in ASDM:
Open the connection profile in ASDM Set the SAML server to “None”. Save and Apply Re-select the SAML server. Save and Apply again This ensures the changes fully take effect on the running configuration.
3. Base URL must be exact The base-url in your Firepower configuration must exactly match the URLs configured in Azure (Identifier, Reply URL, Sign-on URL). Any mismatch will cause authentication failures.
Testing the Configuration Clear your browser cache or use an incognito window Navigate to your VPN URL: https://[your-vpn-fqdn.domain.com] You should be redirected to the Microsoft Entra ID login page After authenticating with Microsoft Entra ID (and completing MFA), you should be redirected back to the VPN portal AnyConnect should download and connect automatically Troubleshooting SAML Authentication Fails # Check SAML configuration show webvpn saml idp # Verify certificate is installed show crypto ca certificates Certificate Errors If you see certificate validation errors, verify:
The certificate was copied correctly (including BEGIN/END lines) No extra spaces or line breaks were introduced The certificate matches the current Azure configuration Redirect Loop or CSRF Errors This typically indicates:
Mismatch between Azure URLs and Firepower base-url SAML profile not properly applied (see Lesson #2) Certificate doesn’t match the current Azure configuration (see Lesson #1) Useful Commands # Show SAML IDP configuration show run webvpn # Test certificate show crypto ca certificates [YourTrustpointName] # Check WebVPN sessions show vpn-sessiondb anyconnect # Debug SAML (use with caution) debug webvpn saml 255 Conclusion The Microsoft documentation provides a good foundation, but the actual CLI configuration for Firepower is the critical missing piece. With SAML and Microsoft Entra ID MFA properly configured, you have a secure, modern authentication method for your VPN that meets current security standards.
References Primary Configuration Guides:
Cisco Secure Firewall & Microsoft Entra SAML SSO Setup (Microsoft Learn) - The starting point, but incomplete Cisco ASA AnyConnect VPN with Microsoft Entra ID (Cisco.com) YouTube: SAML with AnyConnect Additional Resources:
Cisco ASA CLI Configuration Guide Microsoft Entra ID Documentation
summary:
Overview Setting up SAML authentication with MFA on a Cisco Firepower 1120 for VPN access is essential for modern security requirements. Microsoft’s documentation provides a good starting point, but it’s missing critical CLI configuration commands for the Firepower side.
This guide fills in those gaps and documents the lessons learned during implementation.
Prerequisites Cisco Firepower 1120 with appropriate licensing and AnyConnect Microsoft Entra ID tenant with administrative access Access to Firepower via ASDM or CLI Your Firepower VPN’s public FQDN and SSL certificate configured Configuration Steps Step 1: Create the Enterprise Application in Azure Follow Microsoft’s guide to create the Cisco Secure Firewall app in Microsoft Entra ID:

Introduction Managing a small inventory in Excel can be convenient at first—but as the inventory grows, Excel often becomes more of a bottleneck than a solution. I recently decided to shift from an Excel-based approach to a SharePoint List for better flexibility, multi-user access, and integration potential with APIs (like Dell’s warranty service).
In this post, I’ll walk you through:
Why I moved from Excel to SharePoint How I set up the SharePoint List Automating warranty checks with the Dell API Lessons learned and future ideas 1. Why Move Away from Excel? Excel is great for quick data entry, but it shows its limitations when:
Multiple users need to edit data simultaneously without version conflicts. You want to leverage real-time forms or automated processes. You need robust searching, filtering, and indexing across multiple columns. SharePoint Lists solve these problems by providing a web-based interface, access control via Microsoft 365, and the ability to integrate with tools like Power Automate or Python scripts via the Microsoft Graph API. I might build a PowerApp ontop of the list in the future to appify it further.
2. Setting Up the SharePoint List I created a list called “Inventory” within a SharePoint site dedicated to IT assets. Each item in the list has fields like:
Title: The device name or label ServiceTagSerial: The device’s Dell service tag WarrantyType and WarrantyExpiration: For tracking coverage Status: e.g., “Assigned” or “Available” DeviceType (Laptop, Desktop, etc.) Location, Notes, and others… This structure immediately gave me:
Concurrent editing by multiple team members Easy filtering (e.g., all items with “Status == Assigned”) Built-in version history and user permissions Easy Filters and View. I love views in SPO. 3. Automating Warranty Checks with the Dell API The inventory that I inherited was a mess. I wanted to progrmatically update it. So I wrote a scrpt to check warranty type and expiration date using Dell’s API. Here’s the high-level flow:
Script Authenticates to SharePoint:
Using Microsoft Entra ID (or an OAuth client) to connect to the list programmatically. Query for “Assigned” Items:
Grab items where Status == 'Assigned'. Dell API Call:
For each item, parse the ServiceTagSerial field, make a request to the Dell Warranty API, and get the latest coverage info. Update SharePoint:
Write back the WarrantyType and WarrantyExpiration fields using Python + Microsoft Graph (or the direct SharePoint REST API). This automation ensures up-to-date warranty data is always visible in the same place where staff track device assignments—no more guesswork or rummaging through spreadsheets.
4. Lessons Learned & Future Plans Index Key Fields: Filtering by fields like Status or ServiceTagSerial is smoother when columns are indexed in SharePoint. Consider Power Automate: If you’re not comfortable with custom scripts, Power Automate can help you schedule daily or weekly updates from Dell’s API. Dynamic Replacement Flags: A small JSON column formatting snippet or a calculated field can highlight which devices are due for replacement each year (e.g., “Replace in 2026”). Secure Your Credentials: Always store API keys or secrets in a secure fashion (e.g., Azure Key Vault, environment variables) rather than plain-text in scripts. Conclusion Migrating from an Excel file to a SharePoint List drastically simplified my small inventory management process. Collaboration improved, updates became programmatic, and pulling warranty information from Dell’s API gives real-time insights that Excel just couldn’t offer.
If you’re juggling device assignments and service tags in Excel, consider giving SharePoint + some automation a try—it might be the flexible, scalable solution you’ve been missing.
Thanks for reading! If you have questions or need help integrating your own solution, feel free to reach out or comment below.

Repairing my Sena 20S Evo: Battery Replacement & Right to Repair When my Sena 20S Evo finally refused to power on, I realized I had to replace its battery. Sena didn’t make the job easy. 5 small screws, a knob, and a glued-in battery made it a challenge.
I ordered a replacement battery from Amazon:
802540-Motorcycles Bluetooth Replacement Intercom Battery
This video really helped me out:
How to Replace Sena 20S Evo Battery
What You Need Small screw drivers and a pry tool or an iFixit tool kit that has everything you need. Replacement battery Patience and a steady hand Steps Remove the five Phillips screws. Remove the knob using a pry tool from the iFixit kit. Take out the motherboard, carefully disconnecting its connectors (you may remove the water seal for extra clearance). Pry out the old battery and disconnect it. Connect the new 950 mAh replacement battery in place of the original. Remove the internal ledge/tab (you may need to carefully break it off with needle‑nose pliers) so the motherboard fits correctly under the cover. Reassemble everything: reinstall the motherboard, water seal, top cover, knob, and screws. I did struggle with the water seal and getting the motherboard back into place.
Tip: Get an iFixit tool kit.
Why Right to Repair Matters Sena could have made repalacing the battery easier. I don’t have a need to replace my headset constantly.
Happy repairing!

I’ve been working on a canvas app to track and manage major IT projects. The app uses a SharePoint list as a datasource. Our executives also use the app and the PowerBI dashboard to review projects that require executive approval in the form of what we call our Change Advisory Board (CAB).
I received feedback from a member of our CAB. “It would be nice to separate out the completed projects from all the other projects.”
I thought it would be easy to change my filter syntax to include project status of “not completed”. Wrong. You cannot delegate “not” when using a SharePoint list.
Problem Using ‘Not’ in a gallery filter results in a delegation warning with a SharePoint List.
The dreaded delegation warning
Solution In this use case, I resolved my delegation and filter dilemma with a new choice column in my datasource named “Archived” with the values of ‘true’ or ‘false’. Since equals to can be delegated, I make an equals to comparison to ‘false’ to show all active projects.
Now I have a filter expression that uses my various project filters and meets my user request.
I decided to use a PowerAutomate flow to set my archive flag. I have other helper flows for the solution, so I chose to to continue down the flow route to keep my patch functions simple.
Components SharePoint List as a datasource Choice column named “ArchiveStatus” with values of ’true’ and ‘false’ PowerAutomate Flow that sets the archive flag when a project status is set to completed. Code Snippet

SMS Notification PowerApp with Twilio Integration Problem Obayashi has a subscription to an SMS Emergency Notification platform. Access to the platform costs Obyashi approximately $5000 per year even if no messages are ever sent. That’s five thousand to reserve the right to use the platform.
I was asked to take a look at different platforms to reduce cost.
Solution I built a PowerApp that uses a Twilio connector. We pay for the messages that we use at a rate of 0.0075 per message and $1.00 per month to reserve a local number. This solution saved Obayashi about $4990 in cost.
The PowerApp allows a member of HR or executive to send a SMS message selected groups.
App Configuration Components Twilio Connector SharePoint Connector SharePoint Lists containing Emergency Contact Numbers Screens Landing Screen Landing Screen to select an SMS Group via a drop down. Message Composing Screen Compose a message to send. Messages are preceeded with a standard greeting. Counter to display the number of recipients of the message. Counter to display chararacters remaining in message to ensure message is under character count for single line SMS. Confirmation Screen Displays a confirmation of the message. Code Snippets of Interest Displaying the remaining character count from a text input. My text input is named SMSMessage.
"Characters remaining: " & Text(149-Len(SmsMessage.Text)) Additional Features to Implement I had a requirement to get the PowerApp deployed quickly, so leveraged static SharePoint Online lists for mobile numbers. Not all of our employees have corporate issued devices and were not in Microsoft Entra ID. I’d like to query Microsoft Entra ID for corporate mobile devices and combine a short list of non published numbers. This would reduce the amount of effort to keep the lists current. Record responses from message recipients. I believe that I’ll implement this by giving the option of creating and sending a MS Form in the case of emergency contacts. Record messages sent. This could be implemented by writing to another SharePoint list as a log. Additionally, I could display the list as a gallery in another screen.
